A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same T-FAKE research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–F are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original CHARLOTTE and 300W landmarking results, thermalization FID measurements, and regularization, training-modality, and inference ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains original landmarking and thermalization experiments and adds TUFTS/DRIVE-IN temperature-prediction results, image-translation comparisons, and inference timings.

M1.justification: The U-Net thermalizer and its three loss components, probabilistic MobileNetV2 landmarker, label-adaptation network, and sliding-window prediction procedure remain. Revised training budgets and more consistent 478-point terminology do not establish a new architecture or algorithm; v1 already describes 478-point outputs elsewhere.

E1.justification: v2 adds thermalization evaluation on TUFTS and 1,000 DRIVE-IN images, including people viewed from the side inside cars. Appendix A.4 also evaluates TUFTS side-view RGB images without paired thermal images. These substantially extend the represented evaluation domains beyond v1's SEJONG-based thermalization assessment; CHARLOTTE and 300W remain.

E2.justification: v1's thermalization comparisons contain regularization variants only; v2 evaluates Pix2Pix, CycleGAN, CUT, and QS-Attn. STAR joins the CHARLOTTE and 300W comparisons, while 300W adds MediaPipe and removes 3FabRec. The FAKE/RGB-only CHARLOTTE results already existed in v1's ablation and should not be mistaken for a new algorithm.

E3.justification: 300W changes from a random 300/300 division of 600 indoor/outdoor images to the designated train/test splits, reporting Full/Common/Challenging interocular NME. Appendix B.2 retains 100-epoch fine-tuning for ablations but reports a final model trained for 4,000 epochs at learning rate 0.001. v2 also introduces an additional confidence cutoff and background-masked MSE evaluation on the added thermal datasets.

E4.justification: v2 extends regularizer ablations from FID to temperature-prediction errors on TUFTS and DRIVE-IN and adds cases contrasting frontal and side-view generalization in Appendix A.4. Table 9 extends the inference analysis with timings. The CHARLOTTE modality ablation is retained in Appendix B.4, but v1's RGB-only 300W ablation is removed.

E5.justification: FID estimation changes from twenty sampled subsets to five, as stated in the main text and extended ablation appendix. v2's main Table 4 reports means without standard deviations, although uncertainty for the regularizer and thermal-condition comparisons remains in appendix Tables 6–7. These subset repetitions are not independent model-training runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes CHARLOTTE Full NME for 3FabRec from 0.3033 to 0.1009, sparse Ours from 0.1051 to 0.0969, and dense Ours from 0.1050 to 0.1132, alongside newly documented comparator cropping and revised model training. The replaced 300W evaluation ranks STAR and FA ahead of Ours. Thermalization FID values change, and new MSE results show Ours at 0.0353/0.0580 on TUFTS/DRIVE-IN versus QS-Attn at 0.0409/0.1303, despite QS-Attn's better FID. These are revised or newly reported results, not uniformly comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the synthetic empirical patch measure's normalization and summation bound from N to M in v2 Equation (6), matching the declared synthetic dataset size. This is a limited correction to the mathematical definition. The remaining mathematical framework is retained, with no new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a large synthetic thermal landmark dataset, the RGB2Thermal loss, the first dense thermal landmarker, and strong multimodal sparse landmarking. More explicit emphasis on generalization beyond laboratory conditions elaborates an existing claim.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the revised RGB ranking through bounding-box optimization and training-position differences and discusses perceptual similarity separately from accurate temperature prediction. Appendix E adds possible improvements through adversarial/perceptual losses and spatial normalization, plus background-artifact mitigation. Existing limitations concerning label adaptation, shared subjects, and CHARLOTTE annotations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial reproduction information: translation-baseline training schedules, evaluation resolutions, 21-degree background masking, warm/cold aggregation, detailed augmentation ranges and probabilities, and H100 80GB timing conditions with batch size one. It clarifies the thermalizer's epoch convention and distinguishes final-model training from ablation fine-tuning. Older implementation details moved into the appendix are retained; the code/model access link is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for modern translation methods, STAR, TUFTS, and landmark conventions. Section 2 distinguishes RGB2Thermal from Thermal2RGB research and 2D from 3DA-2D annotations. Appendix A.4 adds explicit first-model positioning for generalization across poses, expressions, lighting, and temperatures, refining the existing research niche.

P1.justification: v2 edits terminology and related-work passages, shortens main-text implementation descriptions by moving details to the appendix, and relocates the landmarking ablation to Appendix B.4. Thermalization comparison and appendix subsections are added, while the abstract, method exposition, conclusion, and overall section framework remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The result displays are substantially revised: Table 2 adds training-data and supervision distinctions, Table 3 is reorganized around 300W splits, Table 4 adds comparators and MSE columns, and Table 9 adds timing. New figures show TUFTS comparisons, translation baselines, DRIVE-IN examples, and training augmentations. Existing displays are relocated or revised; v2 Figure 2 also duplicates Figure 1.

improvement.justification: v1 validates thermalization mainly through SEJONG-based FID and internal ablations. v2 adds competing generators and direct temperature-error measurements on TUFTS and DRIVE-IN, substantially strengthening evidence for the central generalization claim. The designated 300W evaluation and expanded reproduction details also improve assessability. Fewer FID subsets and retained TFW comparison prose that conflicts with the revised Table 2 remain weaknesses, but the added independent validation provides a substantial net quality gain.
